title: Unilateral posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome characterized with a long and gradually exacerbating course over 3 years and that presented propofol infusion syndrome – A case report
case_prompt:
A 32-year-old woman with a 17-year history of ovarian dysfunction treated cyclically with conjugated estrogens and medroxyprogesterone presented after a 3-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. For 3 months she had experienced photophobia and nausea, and she had episodic focal seizures every 3 months over the preceding 3 years, managed as an outpatient with levetiracetam 1000 mg/day. Her blood pressure on presentation was 124/77 mmHg, and routine laboratory tests were normal. 

Head CT on day 1 revealed a low-density area in the left occipital lobe. MRI showed a corresponding high-intensity area on diffusion-weighted and T2-weighted images and increased cerebral blood flow in the same region on arterial spin labeling. She was treated with nicardipine (target systolic pressure ≈110 mmHg), levetiracetam increased to 3000 mg/day, and edaravone 60 mg/day. 

By day 12 she developed motor aphasia and apraxia. T2-weighted imaging demonstrated enlargement of the left parieto-occipital high-intensity area and further increased perfusion on arterial spin labeling. Glycerol and magnesium sulfate were administered. 

On day 26 her aphasia and apraxia worsened, prompting addition of perampanel and a course of steroid pulses. By day 29 CT and MRI showed further spread of the T2 hyperintensity from the left parieto-occipital region into the temporal lobe, with persistent hyperperfusion on arterial spin labeling. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI showed no contrast enhancement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malignant glioma was considered as a cause of progressive unilateral edema — “Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted image usually reveals enhanced lesion in the progressive glioma, but our case did not reveal such enhanced lesion; therefore, malignant glioma may be negative in our case.”  
2. MELAS was raised because of focal lesions and seizures — “MELAS could not be ruled out, but laboratory tests, radiological findings of our patient did not meet the diagnostic criteria, and we did not perform pathological or genetic tests.”
